Inscription: Inscription type: owner's mark Inscription position: interior Inscription quoted: NEKKO HORA Inscription note: recutagular sticker with red frame
description: This fragmentary artifact is a sherd from the neck of a bottle, dating back to the Kamakura Period (1185-1333) in Japan. Fashioned from green-glazed stoneware, the piece exhibits incised detailing, a technique reflecting the sophisticated ceramic practices of its era. It carries an owner's mark inscribed on a rectangular sticker with a red frame, reading "NEKKO HORA," positioned on the interior. This artifact was found in Seto-shi, a locality renowned for its historical significance in Japanese ceramic production. The sherd offers a glimpse into the artistry and material culture of the Kamakura Period, encapsulating the traditional craftsmanship of the time.

Inscription: Inscription type: inscription Inscription language: English Inscription quoted: Mino near Kiyomizu 3 ri from Akasaka
description: This Late Kofun period pedestal long-necked jar, dating to around 600 CE, is a striking example of Japanese stoneware craftsmanship. Constructed from high-fired stoneware, it features a natural ash glaze that imparts a durable, aesthetically pleasing surface. The jar's globular body is designed with a flattened shoulder, resting on a pedestal which flares towards the foot, and it possesses a neck that also expands towards the mouth. Artistic embellishments include incised grooves that accentuate the pedestal, body, and neck, with the pedestal itself exhibiting three long vertical perforations, adding to its visual intrigue. An English inscription references "Mino near Kiyomizu 3 ri from Akasaka." This artifact was discovered near Akasaka-cho, situating it geographically within Japan and providing insight into the region's ceramic traditions during this era.

This carved stone equine figure, originating from Japan's Kofun Period, dates back to approximately 250-600 CE. The sculpture, representing a horse or ass, is intricately carved, reflecting the skill and artistry associated with this era in Japanese history. The Kofun Period is marked by its distinctive burial mounds and funerary art, of which this figure is a fine example. Discovered in the historic region of Yamato, this artifact highlights the cultural and symbolic significance of equines in Japanese society during this time, often associated with status and spiritual beliefs.

This fragment of a harness pendant dates from the Kofun Period, specifically between 250-600 CE, and was discovered at the Shibayama dolmen in Japan. Crafted from gilt bronze, this pendant originally embodied an elegant design featuring oval and lozenge shapes, of which only a section of the oval remains today. The use of gilding indicates the luxurious craftsmanship typical of the era, reflecting the sophistication and artistry present in Japanese metalwork during this time. The pendant's origin from a dolmen—a megalithic tomb structure—suggests its role in burial practices, potentially symbolizing status or serving as a ceremonial object. This artifact offers insights into the material culture and mortuary customs of the ancient Kofun society.

Inscription: Inscription type: inscription Inscription language: English Inscription quoted: near Akasaka (Mino)  Kinshozan. 3/10/86
description: This vessel, crafted for serving rice wine, dates back to the Late Kofun period between 600-650 CE. Originating from Japan, the vessel is fashioned from high-fired stoneware, coated with a natural ash glaze that imparts a distinctive finish. Its design features a small, globular body with a round base and a pronounced shoulder, culminating in a long neck that flares into a wide mouth. Incised grooves accentuate both the neck and body, enhancing its aesthetic appeal. A small central hole adds to its unique form. An inscription in English notes "near Akasaka (Mino) Kinshozan. 3/10/86," providing locational and potentially historical context. This artifact was found or acquired at Kinshozan, linking it to the rich cultural tapestry of the region.

Subjects: classical deity; classical mythology; mythical figure/creature
Assoc name: Representation of: Theseus;  Representation of: Aithra;  Representation of: Pittheus;  Representation of: Nike/Victoria/Victory;  Representation of: Aegeus
description: This Attic red-figured amphora, dating from 480-460 BC, vividly depicts scenes from classical mythology, crafted with fine technique and traces of archaism. The obverse side illustrates "The Recognition of Theseus," where the youthful hero, presented beardless and adorned with a short undertied chiton, is grasped by Aegeus, an elderly man with white hair and a beard, who extends a rolled band. Aithra stands between them, elegantly dressed and touching Theseus' chin, while behind him is Pittheus, holding a trident, his figure expertly rendered but partially obscured by the design's border. The reverse side showcases a face-off between a similarly attired youth and Nike, who offers a phiale with grace and precision. The amphora exhibits refined details such as purple fillets and brown hair delineations, with the design encased within panels featuring key, lotus, and net patterns, enriched by a band of black rays around its body. Discovered in Vulci, this pottery piece not only embodies the rich artistic traditions of ancient Greece but also resonates with the enduring narratives of figures like Theseus, Aithra, Pittheus, Nike, and Aegeus.

Inscription: Inscription type: merchant's mark Inscription position: under foot Inscription script: Greek Inscription note: lambda-eta ligature, twice, deltoid mark and 'tick'
Assoc name: Representation of: Herakles/Hercules;  Representation of: Antaios;  Representation of: Athena/Minerva;  Representation of: Hermes/Mercury
description: This Attic black-figured amphora, dating from circa 510-500 BCE, exemplifies the artistry of Archaic Greek pottery. The amphora, crafted from pottery and skillfully painted and incised, vividly portrays a mythological narrative. Side (a) depicts Heracles wrestling Antaios, a dynamic scene where Heracles, nude and bearded, grapples with Antaios, who is also nude and bearded, his hand touching the earth. Above Heracles, a lion's skin, bow, quiver, and sword are suspended, signifying his legendary strength. Athena, adorned in a long embroidered chiton and aegis, stands to the left holding a spear and helmet, symbolizing divine intervention. Hermes appears on the right, bearded and dressed in a chiton and chlamys, pointing with his caduceus. An imitation inscription is inscribed above this scene. Side (b) illustrates the departure of a warrior in a quadriga, front-facing with a charioteer, a warrior, and accompanying animal motifs—a dog leaping and a bird descending. A merchant's mark under the foot features a lambda-eta ligature and deltoid mark, indicating its commercial use. Excavated from Vulci, this artifact encapsulates the intersection of myth and daily life in Greek culture, depicting figures such as Heracles, Antaios, Athena, and Hermes in classical mythology.

This Attic red-figure askos, dating from 470-400 BCE, exemplifies the intricate pottery techniques of ancient Greece. Wheel-made from fine buff clay, the askos features a flat body with splaying sides and a convex top, a prominent spout with an everted rim, and a basket handle. The surface, adorned in the red-figure technique on the shoulder, bears a patina of historical wear with certain portions of the black gloss now worn. On one side, a charming depiction of a beardless satyr on all fours with a bald crown is crafted facing the spout, while the opposite side showcases a bull with schematic detail and pronounced hooves, both figures directed toward the spout. Notably, the underside is marked with a single incised Cypriot syllabic character, offering a glimpse into cross-cultural influences. The artifact was unearthed at Marion-Arsinoe, underscoring its historical provenance within the realm of Greek antiquity.

This Halaf cultural artifact, dating from 6000 to 5000 BC, is a black steatite amulet intricately shaped like a Maltese cross. Designed for suspension, it features a pierced section likely intended for stringing or attachment, reflecting the utilitarian and symbolic functions of such objects in ancient Mesopotamian societies. The artifact's cross shape could suggest spiritual or protective significance within the Halaf culture. Discovered during excavations at Arpachiyah in present-day Iraq, this amulet offers a glimpse into the artistry and beliefs of early Neolithic communities in the region.

This artifact is a green chlorite cylinder seal originating from the Third Dynasty of Ur, dated between 2100-2000 BC. It features a vivid contest scene, depicting two crossed lions engaged in combat with naked heroes. The design is executed in a simple and linear style, with the treatment of the figures' heads echoing the artistic conventions of Early Dynastic III seals. The seal is perforated with a small, straight hole, indicating its use as a means of personal identification or decoration. Despite the passage of time, the upper part of the lion and much of the scene remain visible, though a large chip and signs of erasure are present on one side. This seal was excavated from the historic city of Ur, modern-day Iraq, providing a tangible connection to the legendary cultural and historical landscapes of Mesopotamia.

Subjects: cattle; jewellery; sun/moon; arms/armour; equestrian; devotee/worshipper; planet/constellation
Assoc name: Representation of: Pleiades (?);  Emblem of: Marduk;  Emblem of: Nabu;  Emblem of: Sibitti (?)
description: This exquisite Neo-Assyrian blue chalcedony cylinder seal, dated between 800 and 750 BCE, hails from the renowned historic site of Nineveh in present-day Iraq. Crafted using wheel-cut, hand-modeled, and drilled techniques, the seal displays a vibrant scene beneath a multipartite winged disc, emblematic of the period's iconography. At the center, a cow is tenderly depicted suckling a calf, looking back at a leaping gazelle, while a gallant horseman advances below, guiding a horse adorned with a beaded harness and a triple-crested plume. This complex narrative continues with a kid animal below and a stately worshipper standing to the right, gesturing symbolically. The intricate design incorporates celestial elements such as a star, crescent, and the Pleiades, along with divine emblems of Marduk, Nabu, and possibly Sibitti. The meticulous detailing, from the horseman's fringed tunic and plume-evoking drill-holes to the symbolic trident, wedges, and spade, reflects the sophisticated artistry and religious symbolism of Neo-Assyrian culture. The seal's convex ends and slightly concave sides are bordered by thin lines, completing this masterful piece of Mesopotamian craftsmanship.

Subjects: mammal; mythical figure/creature; arachnid; bird; arms/armour; sun/moon; fish; deity; priest/priestess; devotee/worshipper
description: This exquisite chalcedony cylinder seal, originating from the Neo-Assyrian to Late Babylonian period and possibly dating back to ancient Mesopotamia, is a captivating artifact both in form and detail. Crafted from pale-grey, clouded chalcedony, the seal depicts a dynamic scene characterized by a likely female worshipper with extended hands, standing opposite a beardless deity, presumed to be a goddess adorned with a globular, horned headdress and a detailed, tiered skirt. Adding to the mythical tableau is a bearded scorpion-man, whose form merges human traits with a bird or lion’s hindquarters, signified by distinctive drill-hole markings. Noteworthy within the composition are celestial and mythological symbols, including a crescent and a cross-legged table, along with a horizontally swimming fish and a possibly symbolic dagger or stylus. The seal is currently mounted as an earring, encased in a gold setting featuring a chevron design. This setting was added in the Victorian era, complementing a matching necklace and indicating a sophistication in craftsmanship. Though the original edges may have been filed for consistency with its pair, the caps obscure the seal’s ends, preserving its intricate quarry of motifs. This exceptional piece was discovered in Kouyunjik, Iraq, likely connected to Lady Layard, and serves as an emblem of ancient religious and artistic expression.

This exquisite Early Dynastic III cylinder seal, crafted between 2600 and 2300 BCE, originates from the Mesopotamian region of Iraq. Fashioned from rich blue lapis lazuli, it is intricately engraved in two distinct registers. The upper register depicts a seated figure holding a cup or bowl, positioned before an eagle attacking a goat and a stag, while a hatched ornament elegantly separates this scene from the lower register. Below, the lower register features a table with two figures seated opposite each other, indulging in a drink from a large vessel through pipes, surrounded by symbolic motifs. Unearthed at the South East Palace in Nimrud, this artifact illuminates the complex social and ceremonial practices of its era, providing valuable insights into the cultural and artistic expressions of ancient Mesopotamian society.

This exquisite Mesopotamian artifact is a sintered quartz cylinder seal, dating from 2400 to 2200 BCE, originating from the culturally rich Jemdet Nasr and Akkadian periods. The seal is adorned with traces of now red or black glaze, revealing a distinctive whitish core beneath. Its artistry is divided into two registers of geometric designs; the upper register features two pots and two fish, while the lower register presents cross-hatched lines flanked by a parallel border. Despite a sizeable chip missing from the seal, the intricate craftsmanship remains evident. The seal's provenance is significant, having been excavated from the historic city of Ur in modern-day Iraq, thus offering a glimpse into the intricate social and cultural practices of early Mesopotamian civilization.

This Neo-Assyrian gypsum door-sill, dating to approximately 645 BCE, is intricately carved to resemble a carpet, encapsulating the artistic finesse of the era. Adorned with two distinct borders, the outer perimeter showcases an alternating pattern of lotus flowers and buds, while the inner edge is lined with palmettes. These borders are elegantly separated by delicate rows of rosettes, motifs that also intricately adorn the central grid of the carpet design. Within the square sections, clusters of four lotus heads alternate charmingly with four buds or pods, exemplifying the rich botanical motif of the artifact. This beautifully crafted piece, excavated from the North Palace in Nineveh, Iraq, offers a glimpse into the decorative sensibilities of the Assyrian empire, highlighting the symbolic use of plant imagery in architectural elements.

This Late Uruk period stone artifact, dating from 3300-3000 BC, is a carved depiction of a calf, notable for its functional hole designed to accommodate a vertical post through its body. Reflective of Mesopotamian craftsmanship, this piece embodies cultural and symbolic attributes associated with cattle, a significant element in Uruk society. The artifact was excavated at the historic city of Ur, located in present-day Iraq, offering valuable insights into the material culture and artistic expressions of this ancient civilization.

This stone figurine, dating from 6000-5000 BC, originates from the Halaf culture, which flourished in ancient Mesopotamia, specifically in the region now known as Iraq. The artifact, unearthed at Arpachiyah, represents a schematic form with exaggerated sexual organs, featuring an incised pubic triangle and notably lacking arms. Crafted with incising techniques, it reflects the period's artistic expression concerning themes of eroticism and fertility. This figurine provides valuable insights into the societal and cultural norms of the Halaf people, illustrating the symbolic significance they placed on sexuality and reproduction.

This Neo-Assyrian limestone furniture finial, dating from 900-800 BCE, is a remarkable artifact carved into the shape of a calf's head. The skillful craftsmanship is evident in the finely carved features, notably the hollow, drilled eye sockets that give the object an expressive appearance. Such decorative elements were commonly used in furnishings to signify status and cultural symbolism, with cattle often representing abundance and strength in Mesopotamian culture. This piece was excavated, or possibly found, at the renowned archaeological site of Nimrud in Iraq, a location central to the Assyrian Empire. The use of white limestone and the distinctive artistic techniques employed reflect the rich cultural and artistic traditions of the Neo-Assyrian period.

This Early Dynastic III artifact from Mesopotamia, dating between 2600 and 2500 BC, is an exquisite shell inlay with an incised design, depicting a standing figure engaged in a libation ritual, likely representing a priest or priestess. The intricate craftsmanship, achieved through incising and inlaying techniques, highlights the skill and artistry of ancient Mesopotamian artisans. This artifact was excavated from the historic city of Ur in present-day Iraq, offering a tangible connection to the religious and cultural practices of one of the world's earliest urban civilizations.

Inscription: Inscription type: inscription Inscription note: Inscription of Utu Hegal.
description: This artifact is a portion of a limestone monument from the Third Dynasty of Ur, dating between 2141-2122 BCE. It is crafted using high relief carving techniques, showcasing representations of the sun and moon positioned above an inscription. The inscription, partially preserved with eight lines, mentions Utu-Hegal, a significant figure from this era. The limestone composition lends a timeless quality to the piece, which embodies the symbolic importance of celestial bodies in the culture of ancient Mesopotamia. Excavated from the historic city of Ur, located in present-day Iraq, this monument provides invaluable insight into early Mesopotamian art and governance during a pivotal period of history.

Materials: copper alloy; shell; aragonite; cornelian; lapis lazuli; gold; agate
description: This assemblage of artifacts from the Akkadian culture, dating from 2400-2200 BCE, was excavated at the Royal Cemetery of Ur, a site renowned for its rich historical significance in ancient Mesopotamia. It includes two fragments of copper alloy pins that have been rejoined, accompanied by a copper alloy hair-ring and a distinctly crafted aragonite or shell cylinder seal, notable for its central drilling. The seal artistically portrays a captivating contest scene featuring a long-haired bull-man, two antithetical human-headed bulls, and two bearded heroes in conflict, one adorned in a flat cap and both donning skirts, further accentuated with traces of copper staining on one side. Additionally, the find encompasses fourteen meticulously drilled beads comprised of six cornelian, four lapis lazuli, two gold, and one banded agate. These beads vary in form, with ten being barrel-shaped and three double conoid, as well as an additional copper alloy bead fragment. These objects, found collectively and catalogued together, provide a unique insight into the intricate artistry and symbolic motifs prevalent in Akkadian society.

This Late Uruk stone cult vessel, dating from 3300 to 3000 BCE, is an intricate example of Mesopotamian artistry. The miniature vase is distinctly supported by a pair of hero figures, each adorned with belts, who are depicted grasping two bulls with birds precariously perched on their backs. These hero figures, possibly understood as protective spirits, suggest a cultural emphasis on safeguarding livestock, an integral aspect of ancient Mesopotamian life. Carved with precision, this piece exemplifies the ceremonial objects that typify the period, reflecting both artistic skill and religious significance. The vessel was excavated at Warka, a significant archaeological site in Iraq, providing further context to its historical and cultural dimensions.

This Halaf limestone stamp seal, dating from 6000 to 5000 BC, exemplifies early Mesopotamian craftsmanship with its flat, rectangular form and intricately incised compartmented geometric pattern on the base. A hole is pierced through the center and features a perforated lug at the back, though it is noted to be incomplete due to a broken lug. The seal bears deposits and possible abrasion marks, indicating extensive use or wear over time. This artifact, crafted through incising and perforation techniques, underscores the significance of symbolic seals in the Halaf culture. Unearthed at the archaeological site of Arpachiyah in Iraq, it offers a glimpse into the technological and artistic capabilities of one of the earliest known cultures within the Mesopotamian region.

This exquisite jar from the Late Kofun period, crafted between 650-700 CE, epitomizes the high-fired stoneware artistry of ancient Japan. Featuring a globular body with a rounded base and a short neck that elegantly flares towards the mouth, the jar is accented by circular handles affixed to each shoulder. The exterior showcases distinctive tataki matted paddle marks, a testament to the period's ceramic techniques, while the interior bears the hallmark round anvil marks. Shellfish fragments adhere to its surface, hinting at its historical and geographical journey. This artifact was discovered in the Yasui rock tomb in Japan, providing valuable insight into the burial practices and material culture of the era.

This Late Kofun period kodogu, dating approximately to the year 500 CE, is a meticulously crafted sword fitting notable for its use of silvered and incised copper. This artifact, representative of Japanese material culture, exemplifies the technical sophistication of the era with its intricate silvering and engraving techniques. Discovered at the Shibayama dolmen, it is a testament to the ceremonial and practical applications of sword fittings in the Kofun period, reflecting the culture’s emphasis on craftsmanship in its weaponry and associated paraphernalia.

Inscription: Inscription type: inscription Inscription language: English Inscription quoted: Akasaka, Mino dolmens on hills behind town
description: This Late Kofun period tsubofuta, crafted between 650-700 CE, serves as the lid of a jar and exemplifies the refined ceramics of ancient Japan. Made from high-fired stoneware, it features a coiled knob placed centrally and is adorned with a natural ash glaze, a technique indicative of the time that enhances its aesthetic and functional qualities. The lid bears an English inscription referencing "Akasaka, Mino dolmens on hills behind town," suggesting a cultural or geographical connection possibly related to its findspot. Discovered near Akasaka-cho, this piece reflects the enduring legacy of the Late Kofun culture in Japan, particularly in ceramic traditions.

Inscription: Inscription type: inscription Inscription position: label on foot Inscription language: English Inscription quoted: Misaoyama, Bizen from dolmens. From CSuicho. Inscription note: Handwritten.
description: This Late Kofun pedestal vessel, dating from 650-700 CE, serves as a remarkable example of Japanese stoneware used for serving rice wine, known as daitsuki hasou. Crafted from high-fired stoneware, it features a natural ash glaze that highlights its aesthetic appeal. The vessel boasts a globular body, with a round perforation on one side designed for a bamboo spout, and has a distinctive long neck that broadens into a wide mouth accented by a ridge below the rim. It is supported by a short pedestal that expands towards the foot. A handwritten English inscription is found on a label on the foot, which reads "Misaoyama, Bizen from dolmens. From CSuicho," indicating its provenance. This artifact was found at the Misaoyama Dolmen in Japan, offering insights into the funerary practices and material culture of the Late Kofun period.

Inscription: Inscription type: inscription Inscription language: English Inscription quoted: 1886/2/13 Hattorigawa (Kawachi), Febr. 13/86
description: This Late Kofun period pedestal jar, known as a daitsuki yuugai tsubo, was crafted between 550-600 CE in Japan. Made of high-fired stoneware, this jar exhibits a natural ash glaze, giving it a distinctive finish. Its globular body features a neck that widens towards the mouth with an inclined rim designed to secure a lid, while the pedestal base expands towards a fragmented foot. The exterior displays tataki matted paddle marks, with corresponding anvil marks visible on the inside. An English inscription notes "1886/2/13 Hattorigawa (Kawachi), Febr. 13/86," marking its findspot at Hattorigawa. This piece exemplifies the utilitarian and artistic craftsmanship characteristic of the Late Kofun period.

This quiver fitting, originating from the Middle Kofun period in Japan and dated circa 450-500 CE, exemplifies the sophisticated craftsmanship of the era through its use of gilt bronze. The fitting, a component of a quiver, was skillfully gilded, showcasing the amalgamation of bronze and gold, which underscores the aesthetic and functional priorities of this historical period. It was discovered at the Shibayama dolmen, a significant archaeological findspot that offers insights into the burial practices and martial culture of ancient Japan. This artifact reflects the intricate metallurgical techniques and the cultural significance tied to the martial elite of the Kofun period.

This quiver fitting, dating approximately from 450-500 CE, originates from the Middle Kofun period in Japan. The artifact is crafted from bronze and features a gilded surface, showcasing the sophisticated metalworking techniques of the era. Its discovery in the Shibayama dolmen highlights its cultural significance, as quiver fittings were often associated with the burial practices and status of individuals during the Kofun period. This piece serves as a testament to the artistry and ceremonial customs of ancient Japanese society.

Inscription: Inscription type: inscription Inscription language: English Inscription quoted: Akasaka, dolmen near
description: This Late Kofun period sagebe, a hanging jar dating from 700-750 CE, exemplifies the high-fired stoneware craftsmanship of Japan. The jar features a circular body with one side flattened and the other spherical, lending a distinctive and intriguing form. It is adorned with a natural ash glaze, indicative of traditional Japanese glazing techniques. The short neck flares into a wide mouth, and the addition of round knobs on the shoulder serves as stylized jug handles. An inscription in English mentions "Akasaka, dolmen near," providing context to its provenance or possible site of acquisition. Discovered near Akasaka-cho, this artifact offers a glimpse into the utilitarian and artistic expressions of Late Kofun Japan, reflecting the era's sophisticated ceramic traditions.

This artifact is a Late Kofun period sarcophagus dating from 490-510 CE, meticulously crafted from reddish stoneware. The sarcophagus exhibits a plain rectangular form with a distinctive roof-shaped cover, featuring two circular holes at the ends, each fitted with stoppers. It is supported by eighteen cylindrical feet, with six small holes pierced on each side, suggesting functional or symbolic significance. The interior displays tataki markings, a technique notable in Japanese pottery of the time. Unearthed from the Taikozuka dolmens at Sakuraidani in Toyonaka-shi, Japan, this sarcophagus provides valuable insights into the funerary practices and material culture of the Late Kofun period, reflecting the era's craftsmanship and ritualistic customs.

This Kodogu, originating from the Late Kofun period around the 6th century CE, is a sword binding crafted from copper and elegantly enhanced with silvering and intricate incisions. Reflective of the period's metallurgical and artistic skills, this artifact exemplifies the craftsmanship involved in adorning functional objects with aesthetic considerations during this era. It was uncovered at the Shibayama dolmen in Japan, a locale known for its historical burial sites associated with the Kofun culture, further emphasizing its archaeological significance within the context of ancient Japanese martial accouterments.

Inscription: Inscription type: inscription Inscription position: paper slip attached to pedestal Inscription language: Japanese Inscription quoted: 発掘人赤坂村堤庄八　同村　　　同村松尾淺吉売買人赤坂村清水甚吉」　不破郡赤坂村　々有他　家月見山第四墳台付皿壱固　再度買取人　久瀬村　長岡善蔵　高三寸」; Inscription type: inscription Inscription quoted: Akasaka Mino Tsukimi-yama
description: This Late Kofun period pedestal bowl, dating from 650-700 CE, exemplifies the artistry of high-fired stoneware with a natural ash glaze. Known as a takatsuki, the artifact features a shallow bowl with sides that expand gracefully towards the rim, resting atop a slender pedestal that broadens into a foot with a slightly raised edge. Accompanying the bowl is a paper slip inscribed in Japanese, linking it to individuals and locations associated with its excavation and provenance, including references to "赤坂村" (Akasaka village) and "月見山" (Tsukimi-yama). This piece was found in Akasaka-cho (Tsukimi-yama), offering valuable insights into the cultural and ceremonial practices of the Late Kofun period in Japan.

Inscription: Inscription type: inscription Inscription quoted: Hattorigawa Kawachi, 13/2/86
description: This late Kofun period stoneware artifact, produced between 750-800 CE, is a lid of a Takatsuki, or pedestal bowl, showcasing the refined craftsmanship of ancient Japan. Fashioned from dark grey high-fired stoneware, the lid features a prominent knob and intricate decorative incisions, including two concentric grooves encircling it, with a band of oblique strokes artfully nestled between them. An inscription, reading "Hattorigawa Kawachi, 13/2/86," is present, potentially indicating the site of discovery or other contextual details. Unearthed at Hattorigawa in Japan, this relic provides valuable insight into the artisanal techniques and cultural expressions of the Late Kofun period, enriching our understanding of Japan's historical and artistic heritage.

Inscription: Inscription type: inscription Inscription language: English Inscription quoted: Riyosekimura (Tosa) from Dr.Naumann
description: This artifact is a Takatsuki, a pedestal bowl segment from the Late Kofun period, dated 600-630 CE and originating from Japan. The piece, made of high-fired stoneware, features the foot section of the pedestal bowl with a fragment of the bowl's base still attached. It is distinguished by a natural ash glaze, a technique that involves allowing the ash from wood-fired kilns to settle and create a glassy surface. The pedestal itself expands towards the foot, with a vertically arranged pair of perforations on each side, indicative of the period's pottery design aesthetics. An inscription in English credits Dr. Naumann and mentions "Riyosekimura (Tosa)," possibly providing a clue to the item's historical study or discovery. This remarkable piece was found at the Ryoseki dolmen in Sasawara, offering valuable insights into the practices and artistry of Kofun-era ceramicists.

This collection of five roof-tile fragments, crafted in green glazed stoneware, hails from the illustrious Daigokuden and dates back to 794-795 CE, during Japan's Heian Period. As architectural remnants, these tiles provide a tangible link to the opulent structures of their time, reflecting the sophisticated tile production techniques employed for imperial buildings. Glazed to a rich green hue, these fragments contribute valuable insights into the aesthetic and functional considerations of early Japanese architecture. Unearthed at Nijo-jo, they offer a glimpse into the material culture and architectural advancements of Japan's capital cities in the late 8th century.

This artifact is a body sherd from an Attic black-figured pottery band-cup, dating approximately to 550-525 BCE, during the Archaic period of Greek history. Expertly crafted through painting and incision techniques, the sherd is composed of pottery material. The interior is glazed black, while the exterior showcases a striking black-figure decorative frieze. The imagery features a siren with outspread wings in a rightward stance, confronting a deer. Notably, one wing and the lower body of the siren are missing, but traces of added red remain on the wing and body. The deer’s representation is preserved with its head, neck highlighted with red, and one foreleg still visible. This piece was excavated from the Sanctuary of Apollo at Naukratis, a site of significant religious and cultural activity in ancient Greece, offering a glimpse into the artistic and symbolic motifs of the Attic civilization.

Find spot: Excavated/Findspot: Sanctuary of Aphrodite (Naukratis) (according to Ashmolean Museum register)
description: This East Greek, Archaic Greek chalice fragment, dating approximately from 570-560 BCE, showcases the Chian Simple Animal Style, indicative of the period's artistic conventions. Composed of pottery with a cream slip, the rim and body sherds have been mended from two distinct fragments. The interior of the chalice features a reserved band at the rim with a glazed streaky black area below, adorned with a lotus flower outlined in added white and a red center, complemented by two white bands. The exterior displays a narrow black band atop the rim, a decorative pattern of short diagonal strokes between pairs of dilute bands, and a painted sphinx, with remnants of a red-haired head and curlicue directed to the left. This artifact was excavated at the Sanctuary of Aphrodite in Naukratis, a site recorded by the Ashmolean Museum register, offering invaluable insights into the cultural and religious contexts of Archaic Greece.

This rim sherd is a fragment of a Chian Simple Animal Style pottery chalice, originating from the East Greek, Archaic Greek culture, and is dated circa 570-560 BCE. Crafted from pottery, the sherd features a white slip with intricate decorations on both its interior and exterior. The interior is adorned with a reserved band at the rim and a glazed section below, fired to a red hue. The exterior is marked by a band of dots between dilute lines at the rim, with a painted decoration beneath, potentially depicting a sphinx, as suggested by the remaining strands of hair to the left. Slipped and painted techniques were employed in its creation, showcasing the artistic motifs prevalent during the period. This artifact was unearthed at Naukratis, contributing valuable knowledge to the understanding of cross-cultural interactions in ancient Greece.

This Attic red-figured chous, dating to approximately 420 BCE, is a masterful representation of Greek pottery, crafted from painted ceramic. The scene depicts two youthful but bearded satyrs engaging in playful antics. Central to the imagery are two jugs on the ground; a bearded satyr on the right holds a purple wreath aloft, while another approaches from the left, crouched with one hand resting on his knee and the other outreaching towards the jugs. The satyrs, bald on the crown and adorned with white ivy wreaths, are depicted with beardless yet youthful visages. This piece exemplifies a graceful miniature style, with eyes rendered in profile and the panel encapsulated by egg moulding above and below, and bordered on each side by herringbone patterns. This exquisite artifact was uncovered at Fikellura grave 179, offering valuable insights into the artistic and cultural conventions of ancient Greece.

This artifact is a handle plate from an Attic black-figured pottery column-krater, dating circa 575-550 BC, representative of the Archaic Greek period. The plate, made from pottery, exhibits a glazed streaky black underside and features a stepped zigzag pattern along its outer edges. The top of the handle plate showcases a black-figure decoration depicting a bird or possibly a siren facing left, though the head is missing, adorned with added red detailing on the chest, wing, and tail. The application of painting and incision techniques reflects the distinctive artistic practices of the time. This piece was excavated in Naukratis, an important cultural and trading center of ancient Greece, offering insights into the interplay of Greek art and commerce.

description: This artifact is a concave lip and wall sherd from an Attic black-glazed pottery cup, classified as type C, dating from 525-475 BC, during the Archaic Greek period. The piece features a sharply offset lip both internally and externally, which is thickened at the rim and entirely covered in a glossy black glaze. An inscription, rendered in Greek as a post-firing graffito, is located on the lip, although it is partially preserved and believed to contain a three-dot punctuation. The inscription tentatively names the classical deity Apollo, suggesting the vessel's potential religious or cultural significance. This pottery fragment was excavated at Naukratis, providing valuable insight into the exchange and influence of Greek culture across regions.

This tondo and stem sherd originates from an Attic black-figured pottery vessel, likely a type A cup, crafted during the Archaic Greek period circa 550-530 BCE. The interior decoration features a black-figure depiction of a bird or siren facing right, with distinct characteristics such as the body, outspread wings, one leg, and added red on the wing bands. A series of faded white dots adorns the underbelly, suggesting intricate detailing. The vessel's exterior displays a red fillet joining the bowl and stem, while the stem itself is glazed both inside and out. The underside is reserved with a red band at the top of the stem, accentuating its form. Composed of pottery and showcasing the painted and incised technique characteristic of the Attic style, this fragment offers insight into the artistic traditions of the time. It was possibly excavated at the ancient site of Naukratis, underlining its historical significance within Greek material culture.

This rim sherd of an Attic black-figured Type A cup, dating from around 525-500 BC, exemplifies the sophisticated artistry of Archaic Greek pottery. Crafted from pottery and employing both painted and incised techniques, this artifact features a striking black-figure exterior decoration, with a double ivy leaf frieze above a depiction of Dionysos, the classical deity. The rim's interior displays a reserved band, with the glaze fired to a reddish hue below. The representation of Dionysos shows his upper body cloaked, holding a horn, and likely extending a vine tendril. The field is further adorned with vine motifs, emphasizing the god's association with wine and revelry. This piece was excavated in Naukratis, a significant Greek trading post in Egypt, highlighting the cultural exchange between Greece and Egypt during this period.

Assoc name: Representation of: Apollo;  Representation of: Dionysos/Bacchus;  Representation of: Hermes/Mercury;  Representation of: Maenads
description: This Archaic Greek hydria, dating to 500 BC, is a prime example of Attic pottery, characterized by its black-figure design set against a red panel backdrop, accentuated with purple and white accessories. The artwork features a striking depiction of divine and mythical figures: on the left, Dionysos is portrayed moving rightward, adorned with long hair, a beard, an ivy wreath, and wearing a long white chiton and himation. At the center, Apollo Citharoedos appears beardless with a laurel wreath, elegantly strumming a chelys using a plectrum, while drapery hangs from the instrument. Flanking Apollo are two suggested Maenads, clad in decorative chitons and himatia, indicative of their role as followers of Dionysos. Completing the scene on the right is Hermes, rendered with a backward glance, dressed in a short white chiton, chlamys, petasos, and endromides, and holding his iconic caduceus. The scene is intricately enhanced by a double honeysuckle motif above and bordered by a network pattern along the sides. This hydria was unearthed in Nola and exemplifies the artistry and mythological storytelling central to Greek ceramic work of the time.

Assoc name: Representation of: Achilles (?);  Representation of: Memnon (?);  Representation of: Antilochus (?)
description: This exquisite black-figured hydria, crafted around 520 BC during the Archaic Greek period, exemplifies Attic pottery through its intricate design and skilled craftsmanship. The vase is adorned with black designs set against a red panel, featuring accents in white and purple, and bordered by ivy motifs. On the shoulder of the hydria, a possible depiction of the mythological contest between Achilles and Memnon is presented, where the central figure, possibly Antilochus, lies flat and nude, while the armed warriors confront each other with spears and Boeotian shields, under the gaze of four spectating males holding wands. The main body showcases a marriage procession, highlighted by a quadriga carrying a male and female figure, both robed in opulent chiton and himation, accompanied by figures playing music and applauding. Inscribed with "Λυσιππίδης καλός, Ρόδον καλέ," the piece also bears a frieze of animals below, featuring a siren flanked by a panther and a doe. This hydria was uncovered in Vulci, an Etruscan city known for its rich archaeological findings, enhancing our understanding of ancient Greek iconography and cultural interactions.

Assoc name: Representation of: Demeter/Ceres;  Representation of: Core (?);  Representation of: Aphrodite/Venus;  Representation of: Eros/Cupid
description: This exquisite Attic red-figured hydria, dating to around 390 BC, exemplifies the ornate style of Greek pottery with its elaborate design painted on a black background. Adorned with white accessories, the vessel features intricate decorations such as egg-moulding around the lip and a maeander and chequer pattern below the primary scene. The central artwork depicts a dynamic tableau with a chariot drawn by two Erotes, ceremonially adorned and steering the vessel with Demeter and likely Core (Persephone) as passengers. These revered figures are portrayed with radiated fillets, ornate chitons, and intricate jewelry. Dancing Maenads, Satyrs, and seated figures populate the scene, each painstakingly detailed with beaded ornaments, necklaces, and embroidered garments. Iconographic elements include thyrsoi, tympana, and floral motifs, all indicating a celebration of the divine and mythical. The presence of notable deities such as Aphrodite and representations of Eros further infuse the piece with significant mythological narrative. This hydria was discovered in the Blacas Tomb, shedding light on burial practices and the cultural interplay between art and mythology in classical Greece.

This Attic black-figured hydria, crafted from pottery between 490 and 460 BCE, is a striking example of ancient Greek artistry. The design, rendered in black on a red panel, is bordered by intricate maeanders, palmettes, and dotted borders, with white accents adding depth to the composition. The scene depicts Nike, the personification of victory, elegantly flying to the right. She gazes back, her hair adorned with a white sphendone, while her outspread wings emerge from her breast. Nike's long chiton exhibits white markings, and she extends a white taenia with her hands, gracefully heading towards an altar topped by a blazing fire. A branch is delicately painted in the field, enhancing the visual narrative. This hydria, employing both painted and incised techniques, was discovered in Kalavarda, highlighting its cultural and religious significance as part of the rich tapestry of Greek civilization.

Inscription: Inscription type: inscription Inscription position: on wall Inscription language: Greek Inscription script: Greek Inscription quoted: Λυκοπις Inscription translation: Lykopis Inscription note: Pre-firing dipinto.
description: This Attic black-figured pottery lebes gamikos body sherd, dating from around 575-560 BC, is a fine representation of Archaic Greek artistry. The artifact, crafted from pottery and employing both painting and incising techniques, depicts a detailed scene on its exterior. It features part of a fallen Amazon to the right, the figure intricately detailed with a belted long chiton and a scabbard adorned with added red. The Amazon's face is outlined, with an eye showing a distinctive cornea meeting the upper eyelid. A Boeotian shield with a red border supports the figure, complemented by a spear positioned point downward, and an evocative touch of red depicting blood on the lower chiton part. The scene also includes the left leg and foot of another Amazon dashing to the right, and to the right side, a chain of vertical lotus and palmette with red highlights. A wide border of dots and alternating bands in red and black frames the scene intricately. The artifact bears a Greek inscription "Λυκοπις" (Lykopis) applied pre-firing on the wall. This pottery piece was excavated at the Sanctuary of the Dioskouroi in Naukratis, providing insight into its ceremonial use and the cultural exchanges within this Greek locale.

This exquisite Attic red-figured pottery lid from a lekanis, crafted circa 440 BC, exemplifies the finest style of Greek ceramic artistry. Adorned with a broad frieze encircling the central handle, it features intricate designs such as purple fillets, inscriptions, and wreaths. Surrounding the handle is an egg pattern, while the lips are decorated with alternating sets of maeanders and chequer squares. The artwork portrays seven Muses organized into three distinct groups: a seated Muse with broken away name, Polyhymnia, known by her inscribed name ΠΟΛΥ.ΝΙΑ, holding a likely scroll, and Cleio, ΚΛΕΩ, depicted with flutes; adjacent are Euterpe, inscribed ΕΥΤΕΡΠΕ, and Thaleia, ΘΑΛΕΙΑ, holding a wreath; lastly, Erato, inscribed as . . . ΤΩ, addressing Calliope with a square box. The Muses are elegantly depicted in long Ionic chitons with looped hair, except for Thaleia, who wears a Doric chiton with cropped hair. This lid was excavated from Nola, offering a glimpse into the rich decorative traditions of ancient Greece and the veneration of classical deities in the artistic milieu.

This exquisite Attic pottery piece, a red-figured lekanis with a lid, hails from the classical Greek period, specifically dated between 370-350 BCE. The lekanis is adorned with a striking design in red and white against a black ground, featuring egg-moulding on the cover and palmettes on the body, a testament to its intricate craftsmanship. The painted scene on the cover depicts a lively toilet scene centered around Eros, the classical deity of love, rendered with white flesh, red wings with black markings, and curly hair, holding an embroidered taenia. This vivid portrayal includes a seated female figure with an unguent-box and a cista, as well as another female figure running with a cista and taenia, both of whom are elegantly dressed in bordered garments. A youth, draped in fabric, sits with a calathos, while above him are intricate details including an embroidered taenia, tendrils, and an alabastron. This artefact, with its mythological associations and dynamic composition, was excavated in Puglia, offering a glimpse into the sophisticated artistry and cultural narratives of ancient Greece.

Subjects: satyr; mythical figure/creature; classical deity; equestrian
description: This Attic black-figure lekythos, dating from 480-460 BC, exemplifies the pottery techniques prominent in ancient Greece, specifically within the cultural context of Athens. The lekythos is crafted from pottery, employing both painting and incision techniques, and is adorned in a rather coarse style. The central design portrays the classical deity Dionysos, identifiable by his ivy-wreath, donned in a long white chiton with a purple border and a himation. He is depicted holding a keras and branches with fruit. Flanking Dionysos are two female figures, each elegantly poised on a mule, their hair encased under a fillet and cloaked in a himation. Completing the scene are two Satyrs, each grasping a taenia, with the one on the right glancing backwards, adding to the dynamic composition of the piece. This lekythos was excavated in Athens, shedding light on the religious and mythological narratives intrinsic to Greek society during this period.

This is a body sherd from an Attic black-figured pottery lip-cup, dating from circa 550-530 BC, representative of the Archaic Greek period. Crafted in Greece, the sherd is composed of pottery and exhibits both painted and incised techniques. Its interior design features a black zone bordered by alternating red and black tongue friezes, separated by sets of four black lines. Within the tondo, there is a black-figure decoration that appears to depict two male figures and an Amazon, all facing right, with the Amazon likely turning back. Of the male figures, one bent leg and one greaved leg are discernible, while for the Amazon, a white leg encased in a red greave is preserved. The exterior is predominantly black except for a portion of the reserved band at the outer break. This artifact, reflecting classical mythological themes, was excavated at Naukratis, an important ancient Greek trading post, providing a glimpse into the artistic and cultural exchanges of the time.

This Attic red-figured neck-amphora, produced between 450-430 BC, presents a serene depiction of possibly Zeus, seated regally to the right. The god is characterized by his beard, long hair adorned with a fillet, and an attire consisting of a long-sleeved chiton and himation. He holds a sceptre topped with a flower, and a tall stele on a plinth is situated behind him to the left. The reverse side features an ephebos, or young man, draped in a mantle and fillet, standing to the left while leaning on a crutch staff, his hair neatly looped over his ears. The vase is noted for its drawing of a good period, though executed somewhat carelessly, and uses purple for the fillet and a lighter brown for the hair and beard's ends. Decorative motifs include a meander beneath scene (a) and a row of ivy leaves beneath scene (b). This painted pottery, unearthed in Nola, richly embodies the classical artistic style and iconography of ancient Greece, shedding light on the era's cultural and religious conventions.

Assoc name: Representation of: Herakles/Hercules;  Representation of: Apollo
description: This exquisite Attic neck-amphora, dating approximately from 470-450 BCE, embodies the artistry of red-figure pottery through its detailed depictions encircling the vessel. Crafted from pottery and painted with a strong style, the amphora's most prominent imagery features the mythological contest between Heracles and Apollo for the sacred tripod. Heracles, depicted as beardless and nude, is in dynamic motion, carrying the tripod over his left shoulder while brandishing his club at Apollo who advances to reclaim it. Apollo is portrayed with long hair tied back, dressed in a short chiton with a mantle over his arms. The scene is further animated by the inscribed Greek words ΑΛΚΙΜΑXΩΣ KAΛΩΣ EΠIXAPΟΣ, celebrating the beauty of Alkimachos and Epicharos. On the reverse side, a stark contrast is presented with the figure of a bald, elderly man wrapped in a mantle, holding a staff and gazing backward. Notable features include the use of purple for headdresses and inscriptions, brown markings for Heracles' whiskers, and the transitional detailing of the eyes. The amphora, said to originate from Nola, is bordered by a continuous band of maeander beneath the illustrations, demonstrating the classical deity theme prevalent in Greek art.

This exquisite Attic red-figured neck-amphora, crafted between 470 and 450 BCE, exemplifies the classical artistry of ancient Greece, discovered in Vulci. Made from pottery and adorned using the painted technique, the amphora vividly depicts two scenes elegant in their simplicity. On one side (a), the goddess Nike, draped in a long-sleeved chiton, himation, and saccos, gracefully moves to the right, raising a fluted phiale in her right hand, while a woman in a mantle-tied long chiton accompanies her, holding an alabastron, her hair adorned with a double-wound fillet. The reverse side (b) reveals a narrative of two youths; as they walk to the right, each clad in a mantle and fillet, the latter raises a cotyle in his right hand. The piece is characteristic of the late strong style, noted for its increasingly indifferent execution. The amphora's decoration is framed by a strip of maeander below each scene, a tongue pattern above, and a net pattern adorning the sides, forming a cohesive and visually striking panel.
